newsitem.title: USA: Junk telecom deals return, selective interest seen.
newsitem.headline: Junk telecom deals return, selective interest seen.

text.p: Upcoming high-yield telecommunication debt issues, including some deals fresh off postponed status, may meet with buyside reluctance, money managers said.

Undeniably strong market technicals have prompted several deals back to the calendar in recent days, managers and analysts said, including issues from personal communication services (PCS) provider InterCel Inc and Paging Network do Brasil. Comcast Cellular Holdings led the revival with its $1 billion refunding issue early in May, they added.

Thomas Ole Dial, executive vice president and chief investment officer at The Northstar Funds, said a glut of zero coupon bonds still weighs on the sector. Issuers have circumvented the problem to some degree with prefunded structures, he said, but managers will still think twice before committing more cash to telecoms.

"If it's an industrial deal coming down the pipe, it's a blowout because people have a tremendous amount of cash and want to buy paper," Dial said. "Yet people are so full of telecom they have to pass on them or they have to really offer some pretty high potential total returns."

InterCel, Paging Network do Brasil and competitive local exchange carrier (CLEC) ITC Deltacom Inc issues are all expected to carry a prefunded structure in which part of the proceeds are escrowed and earmarked for interest payments for three years.

Even the inclusion of equity, expected in Paging Network do Brasil and a $125 million Chase Telecommunications Inc issue, may not be enough to entice fund managers into riskier infrastructure buildout stories that have turned in mixed performances in the secondary market, fund managers said. Furthermore, overall demand is questionable given the mass of telecom credits that currently sit in mutual fund portfolios.

"The demand (for capital) from the sector seems to be insatiable -- they'll be back again and again as long as there's any prospect for any financing," said George Edwards, portfolio manager at Prudential Investments. "We've got a lot in our portfolio -- we would consider swapping but I'm not sure we'd be a significant buyer on a net basis."

More widely recognized and established names, such as CLEC Brooks Fiber Properties Inc and InterCel, will receive best demand among telecoms but may still fall short of a Wall Street blowout, managers said.

"They keep trying to run these things and they can't," said one fund manager in New York who declined to be named. "CBOs (Collateralized Bond Obligations) don't tend to buy these and we've move back to issued spreads on a lot of these and I think that's where they're going to sit.

"The sector is in good shape but not in great shape and it trades with the market from here on out," he said, adding that the Brooks Fiber 10-year notes are already rich at 9-3/4 percent to 10 percent price talk.
The Brooks deal is set for pricing on Friday via a Goldman Sachs & Co and Salomon Brothers led syndicate, a source said.

Paging Network do Brasil, an operating partner of Dallas-based Paging Network Inc, may be the biggest challenge, managers said. They said the paging sector is under pressure, and the startup Brazilian entity is, as yet, unproven as a viable entity.
"You may even see them get postponed again," Dial said, referring also to telecom issues in general.

Performance of credits that return to the high-yield market has also soured the sector, Prudential's Edwards said. Brooks Fiber's bonds have traded down about two points since the deal was rumored -- although Prudential analyst John R. Halgren concedes the drift is not entirely supply related.
And uncertainty surrounding the direction of interest rates is expected to keep the zero coupon market volatile, traders and analysts said.
On the sellside, Chase Securities' media and telecommunication analyst Michelle McKinnon noted Brooks Fiber should fare best among upcoming deals.

"CLECs in general have funded their buildout for the short-term," McKinnon said. "This sector does not face the liquidity crises being experienced by several issuers in high-yield telecommunications."
